name: Neck-to-jaw angle (cervicomental angle) theory
lead: The cervicomental angle is the angle between the underside of the chin or jaw and the front of the neck, seen in profile. In aesthetic surgery literature, aging of the neck is described as including a widening of this angle along with submental fat accumulation, loss of mandibular contour and prominent platysmal bands [1]. In looksmaxxing frameworks, a "neck-to-jaw angle theory" holds that a sharper angle in a specific range, often quoted as roughly 105 to 120 degrees, reads as more attractive, and people use it as a measuring stick for how defined their jawline and neck look from the side.

People who want a crisper chin-to-neck line work on the variables that set the angle: body fat and submental fat, chin and jaw projection, platysma muscle tone and skin laxity. Treatments described in the clinical literature include injected deoxycholic acid, liposuction, laser, radiofrequency and ultrasound devices, botulinum toxin, platysmaplasty and genioplasty [3][6][7][8].

The angle is a topic in plastic surgery literature on neck rejuvenation, which discusses combined approaches such as fat reduction, platysma work, injectables and devices [1][2]. Published studies describe treatments and anatomy; none establishes an ideal numerical range for attractiveness.

paras: Wikipedia notes that a double-chin appearance can arise from excess fat or from a bony deficiency in which an underdeveloped jaw leaves the chin blending into the neck; fat-related cases may be treated by fat removal, and bone-related ones by genioplasty or jaw surgery [3]. A review of neck rejuvenation lists widening of the cervicomental angle among the changes of aging, together with skin dyspigmentation, laxity, loss of mandibular contour, submental fat, volume loss and prominent platysmal bands, and describes combining several procedures because few studies address combinations [1].

Surgical sources describe the neck as several layers: skin, superficial fat, the platysma muscle and deeper structures such as subplatysmal fat, the anterior bellies of the digastric muscles and the submandibular glands. Fullness beneath the chin can originate beneath the platysma rather than from superficial fat alone, so the contributing layer differs between people [9].

Anatomical descriptions point to several contributors: how far the chin and lower jaw project, the thickness of the submental fat pad, the position and tone of the platysma (which can separate and form vertical bands with age), skin elasticity, deeper glandular and muscular fullness, and the position of the hyoid bone [1][9]. Looksmaxxing discussions add the hyoid and body-fat levels to this list, treating the angle as a combined result of bone and soft tissue.

Studies have examined treatments that affect neck contour, but none tested the community's stated angle range. A 2016 review and case series described combination neck rejuvenation [1]. A 2015 paper described a microbotox technique for the lower face and neck, in which many diluted microdroplets of onabotulinumtoxinA are injected into the dermis to smooth neck banding and bring the platysma closer to the jawline, which the author reports improves contouring of the cervicomental angle [2].

A review of deoxycholic acid describes it as an injectable approved for cosmetic reduction of submental fat that lyses fat cells and so sharpens the cervicomental angle, and notes that safety and efficacy have been established in several prospective trials [6]. Wikipedia reports the FDA approved this treatment in April 2015 [10].

Device studies include a randomized study of 20 patients with mild to moderate neck laxity comparing fractional radiofrequency microneedling alone versus with platelet-rich plasma [7], a prospective study of 20 patients treated with high-intensity focused ultrasound for neck rejuvenation [8], and prospective studies of a 1440 nm laser and of laser-assisted lipolysis in 30 patients with Rohrich type I to III necks [11][12].

A 1990 retrospective study compared osteoplastic and alloplastic genioplasty and reported high patient satisfaction in both groups [4]. A review of neck-lift complications lists contour irregularities and expanding hematomas among the risks of surgery that gives a more youthful cervicomental angle [13]. Craniofacial photographic analysis has also been studied for sleep apnea prediction, a different aim [5].

Surgical sources describe platysmaplasty, usually done as part of a neck lift, which tightens or repositions the platysma through medial repair under the chin, lateral suspension, or a combination, sometimes with work on deeper fat, digastric muscle or submandibular gland [9]. Genioplasty or orthognathic surgery moves the chin or jaws forward where a bony deficiency is the main cause [3].

Reported risks include bleeding or hematoma, infection, numbness, temporary nerve weakness, contour irregularities and recurring platysmal bands. Removing too much fat can produce a "cobra neck" hollow in the center of the neck, which is why fat removal is described as conservative [9].

The theory is used alongside discussion of chin projection, hyoid position and submental fat as part of profile assessment. Users commonly measure the angle on side-profile photographs and compare it with the quoted range. The numerical range is a community figure rather than a published clinical standard.

card.summary: A profile-angle idea (about 105-120 degrees) for a clean chin-to-neck line; surgery literature describes the angle, no study supports the number.
card.note: The ideal range is a community figure; no study located tests it.

quick.overview:
The cervicomental angle is the profile angle where the underside of the chin meets the neck. Forum theory says an angle around 105 to 120 degrees looks best.

Surgical literature describes widening of the angle as part of neck aging and covers treatments, but none of the studies found validate a numerical ideal.
quick.mechanism: The angle depends on chin projection, submental fat, platysma tone, skin laxity and the position of the hyoid and jaw. Surgical sources describe fat, muscle, skin and bone approaches.
quick.risks: As a measurement framework it carries no direct risk. Procedures that change the angle, such as injectables, fat removal or genioplasty, carry their own surgical and medical risks, discussed in the relevant articles.

chain: Reduce submental fat, tighten platysma and skin, or improve chin projection
Chin-to-neck angle becomes sharper in profile
More defined jawline and neck line
angle.text: The angle gives a way to describe and track how defined the side profile of the jaw and neck looks. Treatments that reduce submental fat, tighten the platysma or move the chin forward change the angle and, in surgical literature, are described as producing a more youthful contour.
